title: The Best Incentive You Could Ever Give
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin clarifies his stance against reward-based classroom management, explaining that stickers and prizes aren't inherently forbidden—only their use as bribery for behavior. Prizes given as a 'free gift,' with no strings attached, can still add fun without corrupting motivation, since they're not exchanged for compliance. He illustrates this with an anecdote about a teacher's Friday 'dance party,' during which the teacher randomly hands out prizes as pure celebration rather than reward for good behavior, and notes that students don't feel envy because the gifts can't be earned. He concludes that the single most powerful incentive a teacher can offer is a classroom students genuinely look forward to attending—which cannot be manufactured through transactional rewards.
points: Rewards used as bribery ('do this and get that') create new problems and don't produce lasting behavior change.
Prizes given with no conditions attached—as a 'free gift'—can still add fun without corrupting intrinsic motivation.
An anecdote about a Friday 'dance party' illustrates how spontaneous, unconditioned prize-giving avoids envy because rewards can't be earned or predicted.
Reward-for-behavior systems create a 'tit-for-tat business transaction' feel that removes heart and soul from the teacher-student relationship.
The single most powerful incentive a teacher can offer is a classroom students genuinely look forward to attending every day.
quotes: Because I believe it’s a mistake to reward students for good behavior, I’m often asked, “So, then, the stickers, prizes, and such . . . should teachers refrain from giving them out at all?
Anything that whiffs of bribery should be avoided. No doubt about it.

Instead of doling out prizes based on what you receive in return (i.e. good behavior), you'll hand them out for no reason at all. In other words, they become no longer an incentive in the traditional sense, but a free gift.
A common complaint from teachers is that they’re under-appreciated by students. But this is a natural consequence of using rewards in exchange for good behavior.
The dance party isn’t a reward, however, and it isn’t a strategy. It’s nothing more than an expression of joy, an uninhibited celebration of another week of learning together.
There is no heartless exchange of goods and services. There is no bribery or manipulation. There is no “do this and get that“ culture to produce envy and jealousy.
